title: Truth and beauty (CCC 2500–2503)
hook: beauty expresses truth; art can raise the soul

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eighth commandment: no false witness, and no spreading of faults, even true ones. Your line was guard reputations. Did you keep one story to yourself? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

The eighth commandment is about truth. The Catechism's section on it covers lying, false witness, gossip, oaths, and the use of the media. Then, in its closing paragraphs, it turns somewhere unexpected. It talks about beauty. About the work of artists, and the art made for churches. A commandment about not lying ends with a word about art. Today: truth and beauty, and why the Catechism puts them in the same room.
screen: `THE END OF THE SECTION ON TRUTH.` → `ARTISTS, AND ART MADE FOR CHURCHES.` → `WHY ART, HERE?`

segments.voice: The Catechism's claim is simple to say. Truth is beautiful in itself. Words are one way truth gets told, but not the only one. Beauty can tell it too. Truth, the Catechism says, can find other forms of expression, above all when what has to be said is beyond words: the depths of the heart, the mystery of God. It draws this from the Book of Wisdom, which says that from the greatness and beauty of created things, their maker can be seen, by comparison. Behind every sunset, in that reading, is an artist. Then the Catechism turns to human art. It calls art a form of practical wisdom, a gift of the Creator, joining knowledge and skill to give form to the truth of something. A carpenter, a singer and a painter are all doing it. Art, it says, resembles God's own work of making, so far as it's inspired by truth and love of creatures. Then it gets specific about sacred art. Sacred art is true and beautiful, it says, when its form matches its purpose: to call to mind and to glorify, in faith and adoration, the mystery of God. Art like that can draw a person toward prayer, toward the love of God. And it gives bishops a job: to promote sacred art, and to keep out of churches anything that doesn't serve that purpose. So a church window isn't decoration added after the teaching. In Catholic thinking, it is a way of telling the truth. Now, the week. The fifth commandment, twice: every life, and care for the body without worshiping it. The sixth: chastity, whole, not divided. The seventh: goods are for all. Stewardship: entrusted. The eighth: guard reputations. And today, truth and beauty.
screen: `TRUTH IS BEAUTIFUL IN ITSELF.` · `THE MAKER SEEN IN WHAT HE MADE.` · `ART JOINS KNOWLEDGE AND SKILL.` · `SACRED ART: FORM MATCHES PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something beautiful. A painting on your phone, a photo of a church window, a bowl on the shelf, the light on the wall right now. Choose one. Settle, and breathe. Don't analyze it. Just look, slowly, the way you'd listen to someone you love. Notice color, then shape, then what it seems to say without words. If you pray, you can let the looking become thanks. If you don't, just stay with it a while. The bell holds the time.
Truth and beauty. In Catholic teaching, truth is beautiful in itself, and real beauty, in creation and in art, can tell the truth and lift a person toward God. Today's word.
Your line: beauty is true. Today, when something beautiful stops you, stop with it for ten seconds, and ask what it's telling you. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: In Catholic churches, painting, sculpture, stained glass, music and architecture are meant to point to God, and the Church asks bishops to promote sacred art that serves worship.
